text:
Calculate the number of moles in 40 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH.

(Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
hint:
Step 1: Calculate Mr of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40
Step 2: n = m ÷ Mr
commonMistake: Always calculate M<sub>r</sub> first from A<sub>r</sub> values — do not use a memorised value without checking.

text:
Calculate the number of moles in 5.6 g of calcium oxide, CaO.

(Ar: Ca = 40, O = 16)
commonMistake: Do not confuse CaO (Mr = 56) with Ca alone (Ar = 40).

text:
Calculate the mass of 2.5 mol of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄.

(Ar: H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)
commonMistake: For H₂SO₄, remember there are 4 oxygen atoms (4 × 16 = 64), not just one.

text:
Calculate the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

(Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
commonMistake: CaCO₃ has 3 oxygen atoms. A common error is to count only 1 oxygen, giving M<sub>r</sub> = 68 instead of 100.

text:
How many moles are present in 117 g of sodium chloride, NaCl?

(Ar: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
commonMistake: A<sub>r</sub>(Cl) = 35.5, not 35 or 36. Always use 35.5 for chlorine in calculations.

text:
Calculate the number of moles in 8.0 g of sulfur dioxide, SO₂.

(Ar: S = 32, O = 16)
commonMistake: SO₂ has 2 oxygen atoms (2 × 16 = 32), giving M<sub>r</sub> = 64, not 48.

text:
An element X has a mass of 54.9 g and contains exactly 1.00 mol of atoms.

Use the Periodic Table to identify element X.

Enter the relative atomic mass (Ar) of element X.
hint:
If n = 1.00 mol and m = 54.9 g, then Ar = m ÷ n = 54.9 ÷ 1.00
Then identify the element with this Ar.
solution:
Ar = m ÷ n = 54.9 ÷ 1.00 = 54.9
Element with Ar ≈ 54.9 is Manganese (Mn)
Ar = 54.9
commonMistake: Remember: for 1 mole of atoms, A<sub>r</sub> numerically equals the mass in grams. Use the Periodic Table to confirm the identity.

text:
A 0.500 mol sample of element Y has a mass of 32.0 g.

Calculate the Ar of element Y, then identify it from the Periodic Table.

Enter the Ar of element Y.
hint:
Ar = mass ÷ moles = 32.0 ÷ 0.500
Then look up the element in the Periodic Table.
solution:
Ar = m ÷ n = 32.0 ÷ 0.500 = 64.0
Element with Ar = 64 is Copper (Cu)
Ar = 64.0
commonMistake: Do not confuse this with sulfur (A<sub>r</sub> = 32). Here the SAMPLE is 32 g but contains only 0.5 mol, so A<sub>r</sub> must be calculated.

text:
A 0.500 mol sample of element Z has a mass of 103.6 g.

Calculate the Ar of element Z and identify it.

Enter the Ar of element Z.
hint: A<sub>r</sub> = total mass ÷ number of moles
commonMistake: Always divide total mass by number of moles to find A<sub>r</sub>. Never multiply.

text:
A sample of element W contains 3.01 × 10²³ atoms.
The sample has a mass of 9.50 g.

Calculate the Ar of element W and identify it.

Enter the Ar of W.

(Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
hint:
Step 1: n = particles ÷ (6.02 × 10²³)
Step 2: Ar = mass ÷ moles
solution:
Step 1: n = (3.01 × 10²³) ÷ (6.02 × 10²³) = 0.500 mol
Step 2: Ar = 9.50 ÷ 0.500 = 19.0
Element with Ar = 19.0 is Fluorine (F)
Ar = 19.0
commonMistake: You must first convert particles to moles using Avogadro's constant BEFORE calculating A<sub>r</sub>.

text:
Calculate the volume occupied by 1.50 mol of nitrogen gas, N₂, at room temperature and pressure (RTP).

(Molar volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol)
commonMistake: At RTP, use 24 dm³/mol. At STP, use 22.4 dm³/mol. The question specifies RTP — read carefully.

text:
A sample of carbon dioxide gas, CO₂, occupies 6.00 dm³ at RTP.

Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ present.

(Molar volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol)
commonMistake: Divide volume by 24 (not multiply). The volume is smaller than 24 dm³, so you must get fewer than 1 mole.

text:
Calculate the volume of gas produced when 5.00 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, is completely decomposed at RTP.

CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

(Mr: CaCO₃ = 100; Molar volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol)
hint:
Step 1: n(CaCO₃) = 5.00 ÷ 100
Step 2: Mole ratio CaCO₃ : CO₂ = 1 : 1
Step 3: V = n × 24
solution:
Step 1: n(CaCO₃) = 5.00 ÷ 100 = 0.0500 mol
Step 2: n(CO₂) = 0.0500 mol (1:1 ratio)
Step 3: V = 0.0500 × 24
V = 1.20 dm³
commonMistake: Always write out the mole ratio step explicitly — even when it is 1:1. Examiners award a mark for this step.

text:
What mass of magnesium, Mg, is needed to produce 4.80 dm³ of hydrogen gas at RTP?

Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂

(Ar: Mg = 24.3; Molar volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol)
hint:
Step 1: n(H₂) = V ÷ 24
Step 2: Mole ratio Mg : H₂ = 1 : 1
Step 3: m(Mg) = n × Ar
commonMistake: Work backwards: volume → moles → mole ratio → moles of Mg → mass. Do not skip the ratio step.

text:
Calculate the volume at RTP of the gas produced when 13.0 g of zinc reacts with excess dilute sulfuric acid.

Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂

(Ar: Zn = 65.4; Molar volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol)
hint:
Step 1: n(Zn) = 13.0 ÷ 65.4
Step 2: n(H₂) = n(Zn) (1:1 ratio)
Step 3: V = n × 24
commonMistake: Use A<sub>r</sub>(Zn) = 65.4 (not 65). Small rounding errors in A<sub>r</sub> values can significantly affect your answer.

text:
A sample of 0.340 g of a pure metallic element M produces 336 cm³ of hydrogen gas at RTP when reacted with excess hydrochloric acid.

M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂

Calculate the Ar of M and identify the element.

Enter the Ar of M.

(Molar volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol; 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³)
hint:
Step 1: Convert cm³ to dm³
Step 2: n(H₂) = V ÷ 24
Step 3: From equation M:H₂ = 1:1, so n(M) = n(H₂)
Step 4: Ar(M) = mass ÷ moles
solution:
Step 1: V(H₂) = 336 ÷ 1000 = 0.336 dm³
Step 2: n(H₂) = 0.336 ÷ 24 = 0.0140 mol
Step 3: n(M) = 0.0140 mol (1:1 ratio)
Step 4: Ar = 0.340 ÷ 0.0140 = 24.28 ≈ 24.3
Element M is Magnesium (Mg)
commonMistake: Remember to convert cm³ to dm³ before using the molar volume formula. 336 cm³ = 0.336 dm³.

text:
Calculate the number of moles of atoms in 27.0 g of aluminium, Al.
Then calculate the total number of aluminium atoms present.

Enter the number of moles of Al.

(Ar: Al = 27.0; Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
hint:
n = m ÷ Ar = 27.0 ÷ 27.0
Then: number of atoms = n × 6.02 × 10²³
solution:
n(Al) = 27.0 ÷ 27.0 = 1.00 mol
Number of atoms = 1.00 × 6.02 × 10²³
= 6.02 × 10²³ atoms
n = 1.00 mol
commonMistake: This is a two-part question. Always answer the moles part first, then use it to find the number of atoms.

text:
A student has a mixture of two gases — 4.40 g of CO₂ and 3.20 g of O₂ — in a sealed container at RTP.

Calculate the total volume of the gas mixture at RTP.

(Mr: CO₂ = 44, O₂ = 32; Molar volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol)
hint: Calculate moles of each gas separately, add them together, then multiply by 24.
commonMistake: You cannot add the masses of different gases directly. Convert each to moles first, then add moles, then convert to volume.
